background.definition: Infectious conjunctivitis is a bacterial or viral infection of the conjunctiva, characterized by edema and hyperemia, frequently with an associated discharge caused by superficial conjunctival blood vessel dilatation.

list.listitem: Up to 1% of primary care office visits in the US are related to conjunctivitis.

Conjunctivitis was the most common non-traumatic emergency department visit based on data from the National Hospital Ambulatory Medical Care Survey database representing 23 million US hospital-based emergency department visits.

In children, the prevalence of bacterial conjunctivitis was higher than viral conjunctivitis (71% vs 16%) based on 5 studies including 881 patients of mean age 4.7 years. In a single study of 207 adults, the prevalence of viral conjunctivitis was higher than bacterial conjunctivitis (78% vs 16%).

Chlamydial conjunctivitis is the most common presentation of chlamydial infection in newborns and develops between days 5 and 12 after birth. It should be considered in any child aged 30 days or less who has conjunctivitis.

Bacterial causes include Staphylococcus aureus (most common in adults), Haemophilus influenzae (most common in children), Streptococcus pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Streptococcus viridans, Proteus mirabilis, Neisseria gonorrhoea, and Chlamydia trachomatis.
Viral causes include adenovirus (most common viral etiology), herpes simplex virus, and molluscum contagiosum.
Risk factors include exposure to infected individual, immunosuppression, and recent upper respiratory infection (URI).
Dilatation of superficial conjunctival blood vessels, causing hyperemia and edema of conjunctiva with associated discharge.
Meticulous handwashing and good hygiene can prevent acute bacterial conjunctivitis. A

An algorithm-based process of adenovirus detection using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and furloughing those identified as positive (44 of 542 suspected viral conjunctivitis cases) appeared to be successful in preventing adenovirus conjunctivitis outbreaks among staff over 36 months. C
Ocular prophylaxis of newborns with erythromycin (0.5%) ophthalmic ointment in a single application is recommended by the USPSTF. A
Suspect infectious conjunctivitis in patients presenting with red eyes draining purulent material or "glued shut" upon awakening. C
Eyes "glued shut" upon awakening suggests a bacterial etiology, whereas itching and/or a history of recurrent conjunctivitis suggests a noninfectious cause. B
Culture is recommended in cases of suspected infectious neonatal conjunctivitis and suspected gonococcal conjunctivitis in any age group. C

Photophobia, severe ocular pain, moderately reduced vision

list.listitem: Important points to emphasize in the history include timing of symptom onset, recent exposure to infected individuals, unilateral or bilateral presentation, character of discharge, matting of eyelashes in the morning, presence or absence of ocular pain, and blurred vision or photophobia.

A study of 184 adults found that eyes glued shut in the morning (especially if bilateral; OR 15, 95% CI 4.4-51) predicted a bacterial etiology, whereas itching or a previous history of conjunctivitis predicted a nonbacterial cause.

Authors of a systematic review found that in patients with presumed conjunctivitis, complete redness of the conjunctival membrane obscuring tarsal vessels (Likelihood Ratio [LR] 4.6; 95% CI, 1.2-17.1), purulent discharge (LR 3.9; 95% CI, 1.7-9.1), and matting of both eyes in the morning (LR 3.6; 95% CI, 1.9-6.5) increased the probability of a bacterial cause while failure to observe a red eye at 20 feet (LR 0.2; 95% CI, 0.0-0.8) and absence of morning gluing of either eye (LR 0.3; 95% CI, 0.1-0.8) decreased the probability of a bacterial cause.

Another study found that children with bacterial conjunctivitis typically present with ocular purulence (91%) and bilateral symptoms (69%). Foreign body sensation, history of recent URI, and concurrent otitis media in children (29%) are also relatively common. Absence of ocular purulence reduces the likelihood of a bacterial etiology (LR− 0.2).

In the most recent systematic review, clinical findings that best distinguished a bacterial etiology were mucopurulent ocular discharge (positive LR 2.1; 95% CI, 1.7-2.6]) and otitis media (positive LR 2.5; 95% CI, 1.5-4.4). For viral etiology for conjunctivitis, best distinguishing features were pharyngitis (positive LR range, 5.4-9.9), preauricular lymphadenopathy (positive LR range, 2.5-5.6), and contact with another person with red eye (positive LR 2.5; 95% CI, 1.6-3.7).
The physical examination should include, when possible, assessment of visual acuity and an external examination of the eye. With suspected foreign body, slit-lamp biomicroscopy is recommended.

Signs and symptoms suggesting an urgent need for referral include reduction of visual acuity, "ciliary flush" presenting as injection and redness in a ring at the limbus (transition zone between the cornea and sclera), photophobia, severe foreign body sensation, fixed pupil, corneal opacity, or severe headache with nausea.

Viral diagnostic testing is not routinely performed, but an antigen detection immunodiagnostic test is available for adenovirus conjunctivitis. A cost-effectiveness study found that use of a point-of-care test with no antibiotic treatment for those testing positive for adenovirus would result in marked savings and avoidance of unnecessary treatment for over 1 million US conjunctivitis cases.

Bacterial culture for chlamydia and gonorrhea and a direct fluorescence antibody test from a conjunctival swab obtained from the everted eyelid are recommended in cases of suspected infectious neonatal conjunctivitis. Bacterial culture should be obtained for suspected gonococcal conjunctivitis in any age group. If suspected gonorrhea conjunctivitis in a neonate, the CDC recommends performing a Gram stain of conjunctival exudate to assess for intracellular gram-negative diplococci.
Consider referral for a biopsy if conjunctivitis is unresponsive to therapy.

Slit-lamp examination is recommended in patients with a "ciliary flush" presenting as injection and redness in a ring at the limbus (transition zone between the cornea and sclera), photophobia, severe foreign body sensation, fixed pupil, or corneal opacity.

Suspect infectious conjunctivitis in patients presenting with one or both eyes red, draining purulent material, or "glued shut" upon awakening. Itching and minimal redness with a history of recurrent conjunctivitis often indicate a noninfectious cause.
Obtain culture in infants with suspected infectious neonatal conjunctivitis.

Consider referral for patients with visual loss, moderate or severe pain, severe purulent discharge, corneal involvement, conjunctival scarring, lack of response to therapy, recurrent episodes, or a history of herpes simplex virus eye disease.

Topical antibiotics (trimethoprim-polymyxin B or erythromycin) for 5 to 7 days are recommended as first-line empiric treatment for uncomplicated conjunctivitis with a suspected bacterial etiology. Multiple RCTs comparing different topical antibiotics have found no significant difference in the rates of clinical or microbial cure. A

Treatment with antibiotics increases the likelihood of clinical cure in 4-10 days and shortens the duration of typically presenting acute conjunctivitis but does not decrease the severity of symptoms. A
Although not well studied, artificial tears, topical antihistamines, or cold compresses may help alleviate symptoms in patients with infectious conjunctivitis. C

Five to seven days of empiric topical antibiotics for uncomplicated conjunctivitis of suspected bacterial etiology: erythromycin opthalmic ointment 0.5% or trimethoprim-polymyxin B opthalmic drops (1mg-10,000 U per 1 mL). Ointment is preferred in children.

Authors of a Cochrane review including 21 RCTs of patients 1 month or older with acute conjunctivitis found a benefit for topical antibiotics over placebo drops on clinical cure 4 to 10 days later (NNT = 8). However, most (65%) patients experience clinical cure within 2-5 days without antibiotics. Consider reserving treatment for children and adults with more severe symptoms or with diagnostic clues noted above that make a bacterial etiology more likely.

In a meta-analysis of 3 trials in primary care populations, significantly more patients were cured at 1 week with antibiotics (80% of 308 patients who received antibiotics vs. 74% of 314 controls). A systematic review found earlier clinical and microbiological remission rates with topical antibiotics although clinical remission in 2 to 5 days was 65% for patients on placebo; there was no evidence that one antibiotic was better than another. A 2008 RCT of 56 patients comparing a topical fluoroquinolone with trimethoprim-polymyxin B found faster complete resolution of ocular signs and symptoms with moxifloxacin (81% vs. 44% at 48 hours).
Topical azithromycin 1% in a proprietary vehicle was slightly better than placebo but only if analysis was limited to patients with abnormal bacterial cultures.

Adults with suspected or culture-proven gonococcal or chlamydial infection: ceftriaxone 1 g intramuscularly (IM) as a single dose PLUS azithromycin 1 g orally as a single dose OR doxycycline 100 mg orally twice a day for 7 days. Cefixime 400 mg orally in a single dose PLUS azithromycin 1 g orally in a single dose is an alternative regimen.

Children with suspected or culture-proven gonococcal or chlamydial infection: ceftriaxone 125 mg IM as a single dose IM PLUS either erythromycin if weight is less than 45 kg (50 mg/kg/d divided 4 times daily for 14 days) or if weight is less than 45 kg azithromycin 1 g orally as a single dose. Azithromycin 20 mg/kg/day orally, 1 dose daily for 3 days, is an alternative regimen for neonates with chlamydia conjunctivitis. Doxycycline is an option if the child is older than 8 years.

In a study set in the Philippines, povidone iodine 1.25% solution (1 drop 4 times daily) was as effective as neomycin-polymyxin B-gramicidin in a group of 459 children presenting with an acutely inflamed eye accompanied by discharge. This is an alternative in resource-poor settings.

Neonates with suspected or culture-proven gonococcal or chlamydial infection: ceftriaxone 25 to 50 mg/kg IV/IM in a single dose (no more than 125 mg) PLUS erythromycin 50 mg/kg/d divided 4 times a day for 10 to 14 days.

Herpes simplex virus conjunctivitis can be treated with topical ganciclovir 0.15% gel (3-5 times daily) or trifluridine 1% solution (5-8 times daily). Oral treatment options include acyclovir (200-400 mg 5 times daily), valacyclovir (500 mg, 2-3 times daily) or famciclovir (250 mg twice daily).
Molluscum contagiosum usually resolves spontaneously, but removal of lesions may be necessary in symptomatic patients.
No effective treatments are known for the common adenoviral conjunctivitis. Artificial tears, topical antihistamines, or cold compresses may help alleviate symptoms.
No effective treatments are known for SARS-CoV-2 conjunctivitis.

Concerning signs and symptoms suggesting an urgent need for referral include reduced visual acuity, "ciliary flush" presenting as injection and redness in a ring at the limbus (transition zone between the cornea and sclera), photophobia, severe foreign body sensation, fixed pupil, corneal opacity, or severe headache with nausea.

Authors of a systematic review of patients with red eye found that the most useful findings indicating serious eye disease were anisocoria, with the smaller pupil in the red eye, (LR 6.5; 95% CI, 2.6-16.3) and photophobia, elicited by direct illumination (LR 8.3; 95% CI, 2.7-25.9), indirect illumination (LR 28.8; 95% CI, 1.8-459), or near synkinesis test ("finger-to-nose convergence test," LR 21.4; 95% CI, 12-38.2).

Ophthalmia neonatorum can result in perforation of the globe of the eye and blindness. The CDC recommends that infants who have gonococcal ophthalmia should be hospitalized and evaluated for signs of disseminated infection (e.g., sepsis, arthritis, and meningitis).
Although rare, topical sulfonamide eyedrops have been shown to induce toxic epidermal necrolysis.
Acute bacterial conjunctivitis is typically a self-limited condition lasting 3 to 5 days. A
Topical antibiotic treatment is associated with slightly improved rates of clinical and microbiologic remission. A
Bacterial: mild cases are usually self-limited with or without treatment. Severe cases may persist without treatment.
Adenovirus: self-limited with improvement in 5 to 14 days.
Neonatal gonococcal conjunctivitis manifests within 1 to 7 days and rapidly progresses into severe purulent conjunctivitis if untreated.
Herpes simplex virus cases usually subside without treatment in 4 to 7 days unless complications such as uveitis, keratitis, and perforation occur.
Molluscum contagiosum may persist for months to years.
Antibiotic treatment is associated with slightly improved rates of clinical and microbiologic remission.
Gonococcal or chlamydial infection also responds rapidly to antibiotic therapy.
For patients with gonococcal conjunctivitis, see daily until resolution. Perform a visual acuity and slit-lamp biomicroscopy at each visit.
For patients with other bacterial causes, follow-up in 3 to 4 days if no improvement is noted or sooner if symptoms worsen.
For patients with adenoviral conjunctivitis with corneal epithelial ulceration, follow-up in 1 week; follow-up patients without ulceration in 2 to 3 weeks if they continue to experience symptoms.
For patients with herpes simplex virus conjunctivitis, follow-up in 1 week.
When conjunctivitis is associated with a sexually-transmitted infection, treatment of the sexual partner is needed.
Instill ophthalmic solution/ointment into lower conjunctival sac.
Wipe eyes with tissue from inner canthus outward and then discard tissue.
Cleanse eyelashes several times a day with weak solution of no tears baby shampoo and warm water.
Avoid sharing eye drops, towels, washcloths, makeup, and pillows.
Meticulous handwashing is important.
Do not treat pregnant women with quinolones or tetracycline. Erythromycin or amoxicillin is recommended for treatment of chlamydia during pregnancy.
